newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Asia airlines to benefit from jet fuel price drop.
newsitem.headline: Asia airlines to benefit from jet fuel price drop.

text.p: Asian airlines are finally getting a respite from soaring fuel prices as the jet fuel market hits a 10-month low and seasonal factors look set to cut prices further, industry sources said.

Jet fuel prices in Singapore, a benchmark for regional markets, are now at $25.00 per barrel on a free-on-board (FOB) basis, well below the 1996 average of $28.00 and after trading at a post-Gulf War record of $34.20 in early December.

Reflecting this and expectations of further falls, most airlines have already scrapped the cargo fuel surcharge introduced last November, but a similar adjustment to published passenger air fares is not expected in the near future.
"There is no intention to reduce passenger air fares right now," said Tan Cheng Beng, Singapore Airlines manager for passenger marketing.
Echoing similar sentiments, Michael Tan, commercial manager, Singapore, Qantas and British Airways Plc, said: "It's too premature. I have not received any advice of a fare decrease."
Airline sources said any reduction would not have an impact on the average traveller as current market fares were already well below published fares.

Most airlines raised passenger fares late last year by three percent in line with recommendations by the International Air Transport Association (IATA) to make up for a rise of more than 40 percent in fuel costs last year.
Airline sources also argue that fuel cost savings were not likely to be immediate as many had hedged their costs earlier at a higher level.
"If they had hedged as much as they could in the past, then the benefit will be minimal," one airline jet fuel buyer said.
Typically airlines hedge between 30 percent and 60 percent of their fuel costs, he said.
Fuel makes up about 10 percent of airline costs.
Oil traders say jet fuel prices are set to fall further as the market is not held up by the seasonal heating demand for winter.
"This is definitely a savings for them," said Vasu Menon, research manager for Keppel Securities.
Regarding one Asian carrier, Singapore Airlines, Menon said the lower fuel costs were not likely to be reflected in financial results due next month for the year ending March 31 this year.
"We should see the savings in its results for the next financial year," Menon said.
SIA earlier said high jet fuel prices had been a major factor in rising expenditure over the last several months.
"It will be a major reason for higher operating costs in the last half year," SIA deputy managing director (commercial) Michael Tan said in March.
But SIA already benefited from falling jet fuel prices when it renewed term contracts in late February.

The new one or two year contracts for the purchase of 380 million U.S. gallons of jet fuel were settled at about two cents below the previous contracts. SIA's annual jet fuel requirement is estimated at 950 million U.S. gallons.
